title: Follow the expensive type across the boundary
teaser: How compiler diagnostics exposed a Prisma configuration we never used.

blocks.text: Almost 60 million type instantiations. That was the clue. The cold compiler diagnostics counted generic type work, not objects created by our application.

blocks.label: Cold diagnostics with Go TypeScript 7.0.2; --singleThreaded is version-specific

blocks.text: The mismatch was in the Prisma types. Our application client’s inferred global-omit generic described every possible omission map, although we never configured global omissions. Across transaction and extension boundaries, TypeScript expanded and compared model payloads under different configurations.
The fix described what our application already did. We narrowed all five constructors and aligned the extension inputs:

blocks.label: Narrow construction and the extension input

blocks.text: Our generated version uses three explicit constructor type arguments, two in the type alias. Check your generated definitions before copying. The `undefined` here changes no runtime data.
The document-number helper also asked for an entire transaction client while using just one delegate. Its parameter became `Pick<Prisma.TransactionClient, "organizationSequence">`.

With the same compiler and cold-check settings, the combined changes brought instantiations to roughly seven million. A type regression check guarded the omission configuration; emitted JavaScript matched across eight implementation files. The useful question: what possibilities are your types asking the compiler to consider that your application never uses?
